atlas.heading: What we tool.
atlas.body: Medical plastic parts are often simple in shape and unforgiving in repetition. We focus on tooling where sealing, concentricity, thin walls, traceability or assembly fit has to repeat cavity after cavity.

items.name: Syringe barrels and plungers
items.hard: Long, thin walls make core support, cooling and concentricity critical.

items.name: Luer fittings and connectors
items.hard: The sealing taper is functional geometry; angle, finish and parting-line placement have to stay consistent.
spec: Gate kept off the sealing face

items.name: Pipette tips
items.hard: High cavitation and a tiny functional aperture make cavity-to-cavity consistency the problem.

items.name: Vial and bottle closures
items.hard: Thread, seal and tamper geometry share one small part and one wear-sensitive tool.

items.name: IV and infusion set components
items.hard: Several small mouldings must assemble as a system; the tolerance stack matters more than any one dimension.

items.name: Diagnostic consumables
items.hard: Fluid paths, sealing faces and optical areas turn flash, weld lines and sink into functional defects.

items.name: Inhaler and delivery-device parts
items.hard: Mechanism-heavy parts trade very high cavitation for slides, lifters, cores and tighter assembly requirements.

items.name: Pharmaceutical packaging components
items.hard: Long-lived closures and dosing parts make serviceability, spares and cavity identification commercially important.

arithmetic.heading: High output only matters if the cavities agree.
arithmetic.body: Cavity count and cycle time set theoretical output. In a high-cavitation tool, that output is useful only when part weight and critical dimensions repeat across the cavity set.
arithmetic.body2: Set cavities and cycle to see the arithmetic. Cavity balance is the engineering problem behind the number.
arithmetic.note: Output arithmetic, not a quotation. Achievable cycle time still depends on the part, cooling, ejection and the process window.
arithmetic.amort: Tool cost is spread across production volume. Higher cavitation can reduce unit cost, but only if melt delivery, cooling, maintenance and cavity consistency remain manageable.

imbalance.heading: A balanced layout is not enough.
imbalance.body: A runner can look geometrically balanced and still produce cavity-to-cavity variation. The useful check is cavity-by-cavity data: how each cavity fills, what each part weighs and whether critical dimensions group by flow path.

steps.label: The runner tree
steps.body: Geometrically symmetrical. Every cavity is the same distance from the sprue, through the same channel section. On the drawing it is perfect.

steps.label: The melt is not uniform
steps.body: Flow through a runner is not thermally or rheologically uniform. At each branch, that non-uniform flow can divide unevenly and create a cavity-to-cavity pattern even when the runner looks geometrically balanced.

steps.label: The split does not mix
steps.body: At each branch the hot outer laminate and the cool core divide unevenly between the two paths. The imbalance is inherited, then inherited again at the next branch.

steps.label: Cavities disagree by flow group
steps.body: Inner cavities fill first. Weight and dimension group by flow path, not by cavity number — which is why a defect map that sorts by cavity number tells you nothing and one that sorts by flow group tells you everything.

imbalance.evidence: Compare fill, part weight and critical dimensions by cavity and by flow path before changing steel.
method: Use controlled short-shot studies to compare cavity filling.
Compare part weight and critical dimensions cavity by cavity.
Group results by flow path as well as cavity number.

diagnosis.cause: Check local gate, venting, cooling or cavity condition.

diagnosis.symptom: A gradual pattern across flow groups
diagnosis.cause: Investigate melt delivery and runner balance.

diagnosis.symptom: Random scatter with no repeatable cavity pattern
diagnosis.cause: Investigate material and process variation before blaming the tool.

imbalance.close: Separate runner-balance effects from steel, cooling, material and process variation before dismantling the mould.

line.heading: Tooling and engineering stop before validated manufacture.
line.body: Metal Form supplies the part and mould engineering, the tool, sampling support and agreed documentation. The manufacturer or validation owner qualifies the process and releases the regulated product.
line.body2: The boundary is agreed before order so tooling evidence supports — but never replaces — the manufacturer's own qualification work.

anatomy.heading: What we specify in a production mould
anatomy.body: The mould specification defines the machine interface, melt delivery, replaceable steel, mechanisms, ejection, cooling and venting before the order is released.

stack.name: Clamp plate
stack.note: Interface to your press. Tie-bar spacing, platen size and ejector pattern are checked against the machine you already own.

stack.name: Hot runner manifold
stack.note: Make, model, tip count and controller zones named in the specification, so serviceability and spare availability in your country are known before the order.

stack.name: Cavity plate and inserts
stack.note: Inserts designed to be interchangeable and face-mounted, so a change is a shift rather than a strip-down.

stack.name: Core plate and cores
stack.note: Where the cooling that governs cycle actually lives, and where core deflection has to be engineered out.

stack.name: Mechanisms
stack.note: Slides, lifters, unscrewing and collapsible cores where the geometry needs them — and not where it does not.

stack.name: Stripper and ejector assembly
stack.note: Ejection is a surface-quality decision on thin-walled parts, not an afterthought.

stack.name: Cooling circuits
stack.note: Mapped and released as a drawing, so the plant knows what water it has to supply and where.

stack.name: Venting
stack.note: At the far extremity of fill. Under-vented tools burn, trap gas and short-fill, and it is almost always designed in rather than added later.

anatomy.classHeading: Tool class is a commercial decision, not a compliment
anatomy.classNote: The SPI classes below are the grammar buyers quote in enquiries. They are industry definitions, not Metal Form ratings — the class we build to is agreed against your programme volume and written into the order.

classes.name: Class 101
classes.spec: Mould base 280 BHN minimum; cavities and cores 48 Rc minimum; extensive cooling.

classes.name: Class 102
classes.spec: Base 28 Rc minimum; cavity and core 48 Rc minimum.

classes.name: Class 103
classes.spec: Base 18 Rc minimum; cavity and core 28 Rc minimum.

classes.name: Class 105
classes.spec: Prototype only. Not a production asset.

anatomy.classClose: Buying Class 103 tooling for a Class 101 programme is the most expensive saving in this industry. Buying Class 101 for a product that may not survive its first year is the second.

wear.heading: At shot two million.
wear.body: The fear nobody puts in an enquiry: a tool that samples beautifully and then drifts. Tools wear. Which parts wear, how fast, and whether the spare is on your shelf or on a twelve-week lead time is a conversation to have before the order, not after the failure.

marks.label: Sampling and correction
marks.note: Dimensional evidence, cavity-by-cavity, handed to you.

marks.label: First scheduled service
marks.note: Vents cleaned, sealing faces checked, cooling circuits flushed.

marks.label: Wear items reviewed
marks.note: Gate inserts, sealing lands and shut-off faces are where it shows first.

marks.label: Class 102 design life reached
marks.note: For a Class 101 tool, roughly the halfway point of its rated life.

marks.label: Beyond Class 101 rated life
marks.note: Refurbishment, insert replacement, or the second tool you had built in advance.

wear.sparesHeading: What should be on your shelf
spares: Cavity inserts for the cavities that carry the critical dimension
Core pins, especially long thin ones
wear.sparesNote: The spare set is specified at design time and quoted with the tool, rather than negotiated during a breakdown. Interchangeable, face-mounted inserts make that set usable in a shift instead of a week.
wear.warranty: Tooling warranty terms are defined per project against the mould specification and written into the order. No shot count is published here: a shot count that ignores your resin, your cycle and your maintenance means nothing.

second.index: When a second tool is justified
second.heading: One tool is one point of failure.
second.body: A duplicate or second-source tool can protect supply, add capacity or reduce dependence on a single moulder or toolmaker. We can build it from your data, an existing tool specification or the part itself.

risks.consequence: A line can stop when no qualified spare exists.
The cavitation chosen at launch may no longer provide enough output.

risks.scenario: A moulder, region or commercial relationship changes
risks.consequence: Another qualified production asset may be required.

risks.scenario: Demand rises faster than the forecast the tool was sized for.
risks.consequence: Cavity count is fixed in steel and cannot be increased.

risks.scenario: A new market requires production in another region.
risks.consequence: Moving one tool means stopping supply while it is in transit and requalified.

risks.scenario: The original toolmaker is gone and holds the design data.
risks.consequence: The tool cannot be repaired, copied or corrected by anyone else.

items.title: Cavitation: how the number gets chosen
bullets: Cavity count follows from annual volume, target output and the available press.
Part geometry, gate strategy, cooling and ejection set the practical cycle range.
Higher cavitation also increases hot-runner zones, cooling demand, maintenance and the consequence of a cavity problem.
The selected number must keep melt delivery and cavity consistency manageable.
Metal Form's documented tooling experience runs to 46 cavities; any narrower scope above that is defined before quotation.
items.source: The final cavitation and scope are confirmed against the actual part, volume and press before quotation.

items.title: Vocabulary and validation responsibilities
bullets: CTQ — critical to quality. The dimensions that actually matter. Naming them changes the tool, because they decide where the gate goes and which cavity gets the closest attention.
DFM — design for manufacturability. The document that precedes the mould specification. Ours, before your steel.
FAI — first article inspection. Yours or your moulder's, against your own procedure.

IQ, OQ, PQ — installation, operational and performance qualification. Owned by the moulder or manufacturer. IQ does reference the tool — identification, revision control, cavity count, sensor configuration, hot runner setup — which is why the documentation package matters.
Validated window and action limits — outputs of OQ and PQ. They belong to the process, not to the tool.
Design transfer — moving a design into routine production. A tool is an input to it, not a substitute for it.
Regrind policy — a process and material decision that a tool cannot make for you.

items.title: Traceability that starts in the steel
bullets: Cavities marked individually in the steel, so a rejected part can be traced to the cavity that made it.
Date and revision inserts where your part allows them.
A cavity identification scheme released as part of the documentation, not held by us.
Interchangeable, face-mounted inserts so replacing a cavity does not change the identification scheme.
Sampling evidence recorded cavity by cavity rather than as one average. An average across 32 cavities hides the thing you need to see.
Change notification in writing before anything on the tool is altered.
